name: Pessimism Bias
description: People can overestimate how likely bad outcomes are for themselves or for a plan, treating negative futures as more probable than they really are. In practice this shows up as forecasts that lean too hard toward failure, loss, or disappointment.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to risk communication, security/privacy decisions, support and incident expectations, health/finance UX, and team forecasting: some users or teams overweight worst-case outcomes and act more defensively than the evidence warrants.
myth_risk_note: Evidence confirms pessimism is real but strongly contingent on threat type and familiarity -- not a universal mirror of optimism bias, but a context-dependent reversal, making 'pessimism bias' as a standalone concept somewhat misleading without stating its boundary conditions.
prevalence_note: Recognizable in risk-perception, health, finance, and forecasting conversations, but the exact named label is much less common in design discourse than optimism bias, negativity bias, or planning fallacy.

findings.description: Comparative forecasting errors run in both directions: participants showed unrealistic pessimism for common negative events and rare positive events, while common positive events and rare negative events elicited unrealistic optimism. The same egocentric/focal processes can therefore overstate bad outcomes in some contexts rather than always producing optimism.
findings.source_title: Egocentrism and focalism in unrealistic optimism (and pessimism)
